Q171617.t: Coffee money, twin motorways and an opera composer
Q171617.s: Two motorways run side by side out of São Paulo and end in a big, sprawling grid on the rolling plateau: that is Campinas. In the 19th century it was one of the richest coffee towns in Brazil. Today universities, research labs and a busy cargo airport have taken coffee's place, and cane fields fill the country around.
Q171617.w: A large pale sprawl on hilly farmland north-west of São Paulo, threaded by two parallel motorways; Viracopos airport's runway to the south-west.
f: Composer Carlos Gomes was born here in 1836; his opera Il Guarany premiered at La Scala in Milan in 1870.
The Anhanguera and Bandeirantes motorways link Campinas with São Paulo, about 90 km away.
Viracopos airport, south-west of the centre, is one of Brazil's busiest air-cargo hubs.

q.q: Which composer of the opera Il Guarany was born in Campinas?

Q5092.t: The harbour that gave America its anthem
Q5092.s: Follow the Chesapeake Bay north until a river estuary splits into fingers of water: Baltimore wraps around their tips. In 1814 British ships bombarded Fort McHenry at the harbour mouth all night, and seeing the flag still flying at dawn, Francis Scott Key wrote the words of 'The Star-Spangled Banner'. Today the old harbour front is lined with museums and moored ships.
Q5092.w: A city clasping a branching estuary on the west side of the Chesapeake Bay, about 60 km north-east of Washington.
f: The Baltimore and Ohio, chartered in 1827, was one of the first railways in the United States.
Edgar Allan Poe died in Baltimore in 1849; the city's football team, the Ravens, is named after his poem.
Baseball's Babe Ruth was born in Baltimore in 1895.

q.q: Which song was inspired by the defence of Baltimore's Fort McHenry?

Q165972.t: Canals like a comb, the Everglades at its back
Q165972.s: Look closely at the shore: rows of narrow finger islands jut into the water like the teeth of a comb, each lined with houses and boat docks. These canals earned Fort Lauderdale its nickname, the 'Venice of America'. A thin barrier beach faces the Atlantic, and inland the suburbs stop abruptly at the flat, grassy Everglades.
Q165972.w: Comb-like canals along the coast north of Miami; the deep-water cruise port by the ocean inlet; flat green Everglades to the west.
f: The city grew around a fort built in 1838 and named after Major William Lauderdale.
Port Everglades, at the city's south edge, is one of the busiest cruise ports in the world.
Westward, the suburbs end at long levees that fence off the Everglades wetlands.

q.q: What nickname do Fort Lauderdale's many canals earn it?

Q16739.t: Oil wells disguised as tropical islands
Q16739.s: A long stone breakwater fences off the bay, and behind it container terminals spread over land reclaimed from the sea. Look offshore for four small islands: palm trees and colourful towers there hide working oil wells. Long Beach and its twin port of Los Angeles handle a large share of America's trade with Asia.
Q16739.w: Straight breakwaters enclosing San Pedro Bay at the southern end of the Los Angeles sprawl; grids of container docks behind them.
f: The ocean liner Queen Mary has been moored here as a hotel since 1967.
The four oil islands off the beach were built in the 1960s and dressed up to look like resort islands.
Together the ports of Long Beach and Los Angeles form the busiest container port complex in the US.

q.q: Which famous ocean liner is permanently moored in Long Beach?

Q62823.t: Where Colombia's great river finally meets the sea
Q62823.s: The Magdalena has flowed some 1,500 km from the Andes by the time it reaches Barranquilla, and here its brown water spills into the blue Caribbean. The city lines the west bank just before the mouth. Every year before Lent it throws one of the largest carnivals in the world, a feast of costumes, masks and cumbia.
Q62823.w: A wide brown river entering the Caribbean between long jetties; the city on its west bank; a large lagoon beyond the river to the east.
f: The Carnival of Barranquilla was proclaimed a UNESCO masterpiece of intangible heritage in 2003.
SCADTA, the airline that later became Avianca, was founded here in 1919.
The river mouth is called Bocas de Ceniza, 'Mouths of Ash', for its grey, silty water.

q.q: Which river meets the Caribbean at Barranquilla?

Q486168.t: A city pressed against a mountain wall and a fault
Q486168.s: The sprawl of Los Angeles runs east until it slams into a steep wall of mountains: that edge is San Bernardino. Along the foot of the slope runs the San Andreas Fault. North-west, a deep notch — the Cajon Pass — carries the railway and the freeway to the desert. And in 1940 two brothers opened a drive-in here called McDonald's.
Q486168.w: A grid of suburbs ending sharply at dark, steep mountains; a pass cutting north-west through them; in winter, snow on the peaks to the east.
f: Richard and Maurice McDonald opened their first restaurant in San Bernardino in 1940.
San Gorgonio Mountain, about 3,500 m, is the highest peak in Southern California.
Old Route 66 entered the Los Angeles basin through the Cajon Pass and San Bernardino.

q.q: Which fast-food chain began in San Bernardino in 1940?

Q81882.t: Latin America's busiest port, under a wall of forest
Q81882.s: A winding channel lined with docks, a long curve of beach, and behind it all a green escarpment rising almost straight up: that is Santos. São Paulo sits on the plateau above, and much of what Brazil sells to the world leaves through this port. Coffee made the city rich; football made it famous.
Q81882.w: A flat island city at the foot of the steep, forested Serra do Mar, south-east of São Paulo; docks along a winding channel.
f: Pelé played for Santos FC from 1956 to 1974.
Santos shares its island with São Vicente, founded in 1532 as the first Portuguese town in Brazil.
The old Coffee Exchange, where Brazil's crop was once priced, is now a coffee museum.

q.q: Which football legend played most of his career for Santos FC?

Q168376.t: An island capital guarding an iron-ore port
Q168376.s: Vitória is built on a hilly island in a bay, tied to the mainland by bridges, with granite hills poking up between the neighbourhoods. The state capital of Espírito Santo, it was founded by the Portuguese in the 16th century. On the island's northern edge, one of the world's biggest iron-ore terminals loads ships bound for Asia and Europe.
Q168376.w: A rocky island in a bay on the Atlantic coast, linked by bridges to the mainland; Vila Velha across the water to the south.
f: It is one of three Brazilian state capitals on an island, with Florianópolis and São Luís.
The clay pots of Goiabeiras, used for local moqueca, were the first craft listed as Brazil's intangible heritage, in 2002.
Iron ore reaches the Tubarão port by rail from the mines of Minas Gerais.

q.q: Vitória is the capital of which Brazilian state?

Q42763.t: Tobacco capital of the fertile Cibao valley
Q42763.s: In the green heart of the Dominican Republic, between two mountain ranges, lies the broad Cibao valley, and Santiago is its capital in all but name. Tobacco from these fields rolls into some of the world's most prized cigars. The city is the country's second largest; its full name honours the thirty caballeros said to have settled it.
Q42763.w: A large city in a wide green valley between the island's central mountains and a lower northern range; a river curving past its west side.
f: The Dominican Republic is one of the world's leading exporters of premium cigars, most of them made around Santiago.
Pico Duarte, 3,098 m and the highest peak in the Caribbean, rises in the Cordillera Central south-west of the city.
The Yaque del Norte river flows past the city on its way to the Atlantic.

q.q: Which valley is Santiago de los Caballeros the heart of?

Q209034.t: Mexico's highest state capital, under a broken volcano
Q209034.s: Toluca sits at about 2,660 m, higher than any other state capital in Mexico, on a broad valley west of Mexico City. South-west of the city stands the Nevado de Toluca, an old volcano whose crater has been torn open on one side. Inside it lie two lakes, and in winter the rim often turns white.
Q209034.w: A city on a flat, high valley; to the south-west a large volcano with a broken, often snowy crater rim.
f: The Nevado de Toluca rises to about 4,680 m, one of the highest peaks in Mexico.
The two crater lakes are called the Lake of the Sun and the Lake of the Moon.
The Lerma River, which flows on to Lake Chapala, rises from springs in the Toluca valley.

q.q: What are the two lakes inside the Nevado de Toluca crater called?

Q17042.t: The working shore of San Francisco Bay
Q17042.s: Across the bay from San Francisco, the giant cranes of the Port of Oakland line the waterfront, loading ships for the Pacific. Behind them the city climbs to wooded hills. In its middle is a round lake: Lake Merritt, a tidal lagoon that became America's first official wildlife refuge in 1870. The Bay Bridge ties Oakland to the city opposite.
Q17042.w: The east shore of San Francisco Bay: container cranes along the estuary, a small lake in the centre, the Bay Bridge heading west.
f: Lake Merritt was declared a wildlife refuge in 1870, the first such official refuge in the United States.
Writer Jack London spent much of his youth on the Oakland waterfront.
The Bay Bridge reaches San Francisco by way of Yerba Buena Island, in mid-bay.

q.q: Which Oakland lagoon became America's first official wildlife refuge?

Q178725.t: The city with the best view of Rio
Q178725.s: Guanabara Bay has two shores. Rio de Janeiro gets the fame; Niterói, on the eastern side, gets the view of Sugarloaf and Corcovado across the water. A bridge some 13 km long crosses the bay between them. Niterói traces its founding to 1573 and the Temiminó chief Araribóia, and its ocean beaches face the open Atlantic.
Q178725.w: The eastern shore of Guanabara Bay, opposite Rio; a long bridge crossing the bay; green granite hills behind the beaches.
f: The Rio–Niterói Bridge is about 13 km long, one of the longest in the Southern Hemisphere.
The name Niterói comes from Tupi and is usually translated as 'hidden water'.
Oscar Niemeyer's Contemporary Art Museum, shaped like a flying saucer, perches on a cliff above the bay.

q.q: Which bay separates Niterói from Rio de Janeiro?

Q49259.t: Watch the road dive under the bay
Q49259.s: At the mouth of the Chesapeake Bay, look for a thin line crossing open water that suddenly vanishes: the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel dives underground at two shipping channels. Virginia Beach lies at its southern end, a resort strip facing the Atlantic. Just here, at Cape Henry, the English colonists of 1607 first stepped ashore.
Q49259.w: Where the Chesapeake Bay meets the Atlantic: a long causeway crossing the bay mouth, a straight ocean beach running south.
f: The Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel is about 28 km long from shore to shore.
The Jamestown colonists landed at Cape Henry in April 1607 before sailing up the James River.
Virginia Beach is the most populous city in Virginia.

q.q: Where did the Jamestown colonists first land in 1607?

Q189128.t: Mexico's shoe capital on the high Bajío plain
Q189128.s: If you own Mexican leather boots, there's a good chance they came from here. León is a big industrial city on the high Bajío plain, surrounded by a patchwork of farmland, and it has made shoes, belts and saddles for generations. Founded in 1576, it now honours two independence heroes, the Aldama brothers, in its name.
Q189128.w: A large city on a flat, farmed plain, with low mountains rising to its north; Guanajuato's hills to the south-east.
f: León is the centre of Mexico's footwear and leather industry.
The city was founded in 1576 as the Villa de León.
Juan and Ignacio Aldama fought alongside Miguel Hidalgo in the independence war that began in 1810.

q.q: What is León, Mexico, best known for making?

Q41819.t: One name, two states, two great rivers
Q41819.s: Where the Kansas River flows into the Missouri, two cities share one name: Kansas City, Missouri, and Kansas City, Kansas, with the state line running between them. The larger one is on the Missouri side. The city grew as a jumping-off point for the Santa Fe and Oregon trails, and later swung to its own style of jazz.
Q41819.w: Two rivers meeting at a sharp bend of the Missouri, with a downtown cluster on the bluffs just south-east of the confluence.
f: It calls itself the City of Fountains and has some 200 of them.
Count Basie's band and saxophonist Charlie Parker came out of Kansas City's 1930s jazz scene.
Covered wagons bound for the Santa Fe and Oregon trails outfitted in the towns here in the 1840s.

q.q: Which two rivers meet at Kansas City?

Q16558.t: Where the West begins, as the city likes to say
Q16558.s: Fort Worth began in 1849 as an army outpost on the Trinity River and grew rich as a stop for cattle drives heading north on the Chisholm Trail. Its Stockyards still keep that cowboy spirit alive. Today it merges eastward with Dallas into one huge metro area; the giant DFW airport sits between the two.
Q16558.w: A city at the forks of the Trinity River, joined to Dallas by suburbs; the huge DFW airport with parallel runways halfway between.
f: Herds of longhorns passed through Fort Worth on the Chisholm Trail from the late 1860s.
DFW Airport, between Fort Worth and Dallas, covers more ground than Manhattan.
The Stockyards still stage a small cattle drive down the street twice a day.

q.q: What is Fort Worth's nickname?

Q6346.t: A planned capital with a racetrack you can spot
Q6346.s: Indianapolis was drawn on paper in 1821: a 'Mile Square' at the centre with four diagonal avenues cutting across the grid. It sits almost in the middle of flat, farmed Indiana, which is why it calls itself the Crossroads of America. North-west of downtown, a big oval stands out — the Speedway, home of the Indianapolis 500 since 1911.
Q6346.w: A city on flat farmland with motorways radiating like spokes; a large oval racetrack north-west of the centre.
f: The Indianapolis 500 has been raced at the Speedway since 1911.
The Speedway's oval is about 4 km around, big enough to pick out from cruise on a clear day.
The White River runs through the city from north to south-west.

q.q: Which famous race is held in Indianapolis every May?

Q49233.t: A city of round lakes and theme parks
Q49233.s: Count the lakes: Orlando is freckled with dozens of round blue ponds, many of them old sinkholes where the limestone below gave way. Until the late 1960s this was a quiet citrus town in central Florida. Then Walt Disney World opened south-west of the city in 1971, and Orlando became one of the most visited places on the planet.
Q49233.w: A city scattered with many small round lakes in flat central Florida; big theme-park complexes and resorts to the south-west.
f: Walt Disney World opened in 1971; it covers an area about the size of San Francisco.
Many of the region's round lakes formed as sinkholes in the limestone bedrock.
Kennedy Space Center lies about 80 km east, on the Atlantic coast.

q.q: What formed many of Orlando's round lakes?

Q26590.t: Half of a desert metropolis split by a river
Q26590.s: In the Chihuahuan Desert, a narrow river divides one large city between two countries: Ciudad Juárez in Mexico on the south bank, El Paso in Texas on the north. For centuries this was the 'pass of the north', a gap in the mountains on the royal road from Mexico City to Santa Fe. Factories making goods for export now ring the city.
Q26590.w: A large grid on the desert on the south bank of the Rio Grande, facing El Paso and the dark Franklin Mountains across the river.
f: Until 1888 the city was called El Paso del Norte; it was renamed after President Benito Juárez.
The mission of Our Lady of Guadalupe, founded in 1659, is the city's oldest building.
Together with El Paso it forms one of the largest cross-border urban areas in the world.

q.q: What was Ciudad Juárez called before 1888?

Q18383.t: A refuge for free thinkers at the head of a bay
Q18383.s: Narragansett Bay narrows northward to a point, and there sits Providence, the capital of tiny Rhode Island. Roger Williams founded it in 1636 after being expelled from Massachusetts for his beliefs, and he promised freedom of conscience to all. Later it grew rich on trade and jewellery making. Two small rivers meet in its compact downtown.
Q18383.w: The northern tip of a long bay with islands; a compact city at its head, and Boston about 80 km to the north-east.
f: Roger Williams named the settlement for God's 'merciful providence' in finding him a refuge.
Brown University, founded in 1764, is one of the oldest in the United States.
On summer evenings, WaterFire sets dozens of bonfires burning on the rivers downtown.

q.q: Who founded Providence in 1636?
